Eight watches, nine years

Nine years, one watch at a time. A few crossed oceans before they crossed my wrist. One was worn on a day I don’t discuss in specifications. The last came with no history at all, and took over anyway.

8watches
4countries
6mechanical

Nine years of mornings began here.

2017

Timex Weekender

Reference T2P142

The one that opened the door.

Movement
Quartz
Case
38 mm brass
Strap
Striped nylon, slip-through

Ordered online for very little. Neither fact has ever mattered. The Weekender descends from the plain, legible watches Timex built by the million for people who needed to know the time and nothing else: a matt dial, full Arabic numerals, hands readable at a glance in a moving vehicle. It has never once failed. Nine years on it still sits in the same box as the Alpinist and the Hamilton, and it has earned the place. Everything I later came to value in a watch was already here, in the first one I owned.

Calibre 7S26. Display caseback.

2019

Seiko 5 SNK793

Blue dial, day-date, exhibition caseback

The first watch that ran on its own.

Movement
Seiko 7S26 automatic
Jewels
21
Case
37 mm steel

A gift, and the one that turned an object into a mechanism. The 7S26 neither hand-winds nor hacks; it is a plain industrial automatic built to be dependable rather than admired. Seiko put a window in the caseback anyway, and that window is where a great many people’s interest in watchmaking begins. Mine did. You wind it by moving. Once you have watched the rotor turn, a quartz watch is never quite the same thing again.

The one I would grab first if the building were on fire.

2021

Hamilton Khaki Field Auto 38

Reference H70455533

Bought as a watch. Became an heirloom the same year.

Movement
H-10 automatic
Power reserve
80 hours
Case
38 mm steel
Dial
Black, 12- and 24-hour

My first serious Swiss mechanical, chosen with more care than anything before it. The H-10 runs eighty hours from a full wind, and the 38 mm case is the size a field watch was always meant to be, which is why it has aged better than most of what stood beside it. None of that is why it matters. It was on my wrist for the one morning I would least want to relive without it, and no specification on this list will ever outrank that sentence.

Domed crystal. Calibre F6724.

2022

Orient Bambino Version 2

Reference AC00009N0

The first watch bought for how it looked rather than what it did.

Movement
Orient F6724 automatic
Crystal
Domed mineral
Case
40.5 mm steel

Every collection reaches the point where a field watch will not do, and this is where mine did. Orient makes its own movements, which is uncommon and worth admiring on its own terms, and the Bambino’s domed crystal bends the dial away at its edge in a way no flat sapphire can imitate. It is the least practical watch I own and the first I chose for how it looked rather than what it could withstand.

The one I keep reaching for.

2023

Seiko 5 SNK803

Beige dial, 24-hour inner track

A deliberate return to something plain.

Movement
Seiko 7S26 automatic
Case
37 mm steel
Strap
Khaki canvas

Two years after the Hamilton, another Seiko 5, and welcome. This is the generation that earned a devoted following: a soft beige dial, an inner twenty-four-hour track, a movement designed to be left alone for years at a time. There is nothing to protect and nothing to prove, which is exactly why it keeps being picked up.

Quartz, digital and completely unbothered.

2024

Casio A168

Steel bracelet, LCD, illuminator

Proof that none of this was ever about status.

Movement
Quartz, digital
Case
36.3 × 38.6 mm steel
Lineage
1980s Casio design

Entirely unembarrassed to sit between Swiss and Japanese automatics, the A168 is one of the most widely recognised watch designs ever made, and it has outlived most of what was taken more seriously at the time. Some mornings it is simply the right watch. A rule of collecting that cannot accommodate that is a rule about status, not about watches.

Cathedral hands. Internal compass bezel.

2025

Seiko Prospex Alpinist

Green dial, inner rotating compass ring

The first one I read about before buying.

Movement
Automatic, 6R series
Lineage
Seiko Laurel Alpinist, 1959
Crown
Second crown at 4 for bezel

The Alpinist descends from a watch Seiko built in 1959 for Japanese mountaineers, and the modern Prospex versions kept what made it recognisable: cathedral hands, an internal compass ring turned by a second crown and a green nobody else was using. This is the first watch I read about before buying rather than after. The seven before it were not chosen that way.

Serviced in Kathmandu. Running again.

2026

West End Watch Co. Secundus

Hand-wound pocket watch, date unknown

The only one with a life before mine.

Movement
Manual wind, serviced
Origin
Swiss-made, South Asian market
Provenance
None recorded

West End built almost its entire business around India and the wider region, with agents in Bombay and Calcutta selling to soldiers, engineers and civil servants across the subcontinent. This one arrived with nothing: no papers, no owner anyone could name, no date. It barely ran. I had the movement serviced, wrote to Switzerland and went through eighty-year-old newsprint until part of the answer turned up.

Eight mechanisms, nine years, and one city that has kept time with all of them: Kathmandu, 2017 to 2026.

© Anuj Chaulagain

A note on the collection

What eight watches
add up to

Nine years of buying slowly, and what became visible only when I laid them out in order.

Set them on a table in the order they arrived and a shape appears that I never planned.

A simple quartz watch. Then a mechanical one, discovered almost by accident. Then a serious Swiss field watch, a dress watch, a return to something plain, a digital watch bought by nobody’s logic but affection, an enthusiast’s Seiko chosen deliberately and finally an object from the 1930s or 1940s whose worth to me has nothing whatever to do with what it would fetch.

It does not look like a list worked through. It looks like somebody finding out what he likes.

Character before prestige

Nothing in this box announces itself. A Khaki Field is not bought to be recognised across a room. Neither is a Bambino, nor an SNK803. Even the Alpinist, which has as devoted a following as any watch Seiko makes, still reads to most people as simply a Seiko.

It is the strongest thread running through all eight. The pleasure is in knowing what is on the wrist. It does not require anyone else to know.

A watch that needs to be recognised is doing a different job from a watch that needs to be read.

Proportion, not presence

The 38 mm Hamilton gives it away. It was bought during a stretch when mainstream cases had grown to 42, 44, 46 millimetres and beyond, at a time when field watches had historically never been anything of the sort. They were sized to be read at a glance and forgotten the rest of the time.

The two Seiko 5s say the same thing at 37 mm. The Casio is small by any modern measure. The Alpinist is distinctive without being large. Nowhere in the collection is there a skeletonised dial, a complication for its own sake or a case chosen for the space it occupies.

What is left, once you take those away, is a fairly precise set of preferences: legibility, proportion, mechanical interest, history and the sense that the thing was designed to be used.

The map I drew without meaning to

Eight watches is not many. These eight cover a surprising amount of ground.

Casual quartzTimex Weekender
Everyday automaticSeiko 5 SNK793
Swiss field watchHamilton Khaki Field
Dress automaticOrient Bambino
Japanese field automaticSeiko 5 SNK803
Digital quartzCasio A168
Mechanical tool watchSeiko Alpinist
Vintage pocket watchWest End Secundus

Not eight versions of the same sports watch. Each one exists for a reason the others cannot cover.

Three Seikos, which are not repetition

On paper three Seikos looks like a lack of imagination. In the hand they occupy entirely different positions, and together they trace the whole arc in miniature.

The SNK793 is the classic affordable Seiko 5, the formula that has introduced more people to mechanical watches than any advertising campaign ever managed. The SNK803 is the same movement wearing the soft military dress that made that generation beloved. The Alpinist is a deliberate step upward in finishing, identity and intent.

Discovering automatic watches. Learning to love mechanical ones that asked little in return. Then choosing, knowingly, the one I actually wanted. That is the collection in three watches.

The heirloom I made by accident

The Hamilton will outlast its specification. Eighty-hour power reserve, H-10 movement, 38 mm steel: all true, all beside the point.

I wore it at my wedding. That is the mechanism by which an ordinary production watch becomes something else entirely, and it cannot be bought. In forty years nobody in my family will ask what it cost. They will say it was the watch he wore that day, and that will be the whole of its value.

The industry sells the idea of an heirloom at considerable expense. You make one by wearing a watch on the right morning.

On hierarchy and on pleasure

The Casio A168 sits, horologically, at the opposite end of the spectrum from a finished Swiss mechanical watch: mass-produced, quartz, digital, built to a design that has never needed updating. It is also an icon that has outlasted a good deal of what was taken more seriously when it appeared. Some mornings it is simply the right watch to put on.

The Seiko 7S26 is not haute horlogerie either. It was designed to be a robust industrial automatic that would run for years without attention, and it does exactly that. Judged against a hand-finished movement it is nothing. Judged against what it was built to do, it is close to perfect.

Both of those are horology. So are railway watches, military watches, the anchor escapement, the pocket watch and the bevelled anglage that takes a craftsman a day to cut by hand. Restricting one’s appreciation to only the most celebrated end of that range is not connoisseurship. It is just fashion.

I have spent a great deal of time studying Patek, Vacheron, Audemars Piguet and Lange. A Lange movement can stop you where you stand. A Vacheron carries centuries of accumulated method in its finishing. I do not need to own one to understand why. Buying something because a hierarchy told me it was better would make this collection less mine, not more.

You can love a watch without needing to possess it. That may be the healthiest thing an enthusiast ever learns.

The thing itself

All of the above is talk. Underneath it there is only a spring unwinding at a rate something has been built to control, which is the whole of watchmaking and the reason any of this holds my attention.

The Secundus, drawn from the watch and set to the time where you are. The small hand at six advances once a second, the way it does on the table beside me.

Four things running underneath

Memory

A wedding. Friends in three countries. Particular years of my life, wearable.

Usefulness

Almost everything here was originally designed to be used rather than displayed.

Mechanical curiosity

The exhibition caseback on a cheap Seiko was the beginning of an interest in the machine itself.

History

Hamilton’s field-watch lineage, the 1959 Alpinist, Casio’s digital era and now a Swiss name written for Bombay and Calcutta.

The chronology, in eight lines

2017

I bought a watch.

2019

I discovered that a watch could run on its own.

2021

I bought a serious mechanical watch, and wore it on a day I still think about.

2022

I discovered dress watches.

2023

I went back to something simple, on purpose.

2024

I accepted that a great watch need not be mechanical at all.

2025

I bought the one I had been reading about for a year.

2026

I bought a watch nobody could explain, and spent months trying to.

That last line is where an inventory turns into something worth writing down.

If I had to say it in one sentence

A modest, deliberate collection of practical watches, gathered through friendships, milestones and curiosity, which turned somewhere along the way from wearing watches into caring about watchmaking.

I am in no hurry to make it nine. Eight watches in, there is something here that a great many larger collections never manage: not one of them is filler. Every single one means something, and I can tell you exactly what.

© Anuj Chaulagain

Who kept these

The one behind
the glass

An engineer in Kathmandu with a habit of taking small machines apart to find out why they matter.

My name is Anuj Chaulagain, and none of this began as a plan.

I am an engineer by profession, which is either the reason I ended up caring this much about small mechanisms, or the explanation I reach for afterward. Either way, the instinct is the same at work and on my wrist: open the thing up, find out how it actually functions, and only then decide whether it deserves the attention it is getting.

The collection on this site started in 2017 with no intention of becoming one. Eight watches and nine years later, somewhere in the middle of writing all of this down, is roughly when a habit turned into a project.

Why a compendium, not a collection page

A collection is a list. A compendium keeps working after the list is finished — it asks where each entry came from, what it is actually made of, and what still is not known. That last part matters most to me. The Secundus on this site is left deliberately unresolved: I would rather publish an honest question mark than a comfortable guess.

If you know something about a 1930s or 1940s West End Secundus that I do not, or you simply keep time in a way you think I would find interesting, I would like to hear about it.

West End Watch Co. of Bienne, Bombay and Calcutta

The Secundus

An open-face pocket watch that arrived with no papers, no owner and no date, and the paper trail that gave part of it back.

I bought a watch that nobody could tell me anything about.

Nickel case, worn thin at the edges. A white enamel dial, spotted and stained by however many decades it has been exposed to, with large Arabic numerals and blued spade hands. A small seconds register at six o’clock, and below it, in letters small enough to miss, Swiss Made. Printed across the upper half in fine black lettering, two names: West End Watch Co. and Secundus.

No box that belonged to it. No receipt. No previous owner I could name. No year. For nine years I had been putting together a collection where every watch came with its own story attached: a friend in Australia, a wedding, a trip someone made carrying it home in hand luggage. This one came with nothing but a question, and I bought it anyway.

It stopped being an old watch and became a problem worth solving.

It was trying to run

Before any of the history could matter, there was a more immediate question. Would it go?

It would, briefly. It ran for a while and then stopped. And its behaviour depended on how it was lying. Flat on a table it kept going; held upright it gave up. Anyone who has spent time around old mechanical movements knows what positional behaviour like that suggests: wear in the pivots, something wrong with the balance or the endshake, oil that dried out decades ago, a mainspring no longer delivering the torque it once did.

But the fault was not the interesting part. The interesting part was that it was not inert. Something inside it was still trying.

That took it to a watchmaker in Kathmandu, a man with forty-four years at the bench who did not need any of it explained to him. The movement was opened, examined, cleaned. Old lubrication out, fresh lubrication in. The mainspring cleaned. One screw was damaged and no correct replacement could be found, so another was adapted and modified until it did the job.

Nothing was done to make the watch look new. That was never the point. The case is still original nickel, still marked by whatever it went through in the decades I know nothing about, and it will stay that way. Making an old object look untouched is a way of deleting its life. The only aim was to make the mechanism work again.

And it does. Not perfectly. After a full day it runs several minutes fast, and regulation is a conversation for later, once a freshly serviced movement has settled. But the mainspring stores energy, the train turns, the escapement releases it, the balance swings and the small seconds hand advances.

After however many silent years, that was enough.

I wrote to Switzerland

On the first of September I sent West End Watch Co. an email with photographs of the dial, the movement and both sides of the caseback, the two numbers I could find and a question I did not expect anyone to answer: was this yours, and can you tell me when it was made?

They replied the same evening.

West End Watch Co., Switzerland. Reply of 1 September 2026

Dear Sir,

Thank you for the message and pictures.

Maybe you know that in Latin language, SECUNDUS literally means:

  1. (nautical) favorable, fair
  2. (military) fortunate, lucky, victorious, successful

This name was chosen according to the “military roots” of the brand. You’re right, West End was initially created for the Britain’s Indian market.

The brand provided professional watches for engineers and civil service, and mostly for soldiers from WWI. They liked their sturdiness and dependability!

Secundus brand was launched in the 1930’s as pocket watches as well as wrist watches, more convenient for soldiers for example.

Unfortunately, we don’t have more details about this watch since our archives are held in a museum not in our factory but we hope that this information will still be helpful.

Congratulations for treasuring this old pocket watch and preserving its historical value.

With best regards from Switzerland.

Reproduced as received. Signed WEW / Sandra, sent from the company’s office in Switzerland.

One line in that message did more work than everything else I had found. The Secundus brand was launched in the 1930s.

I had gone into this half-believing something else. My own email to them carried the words “possibly WWI era” in the subject line, because that is what the internet had told me, in modern listings describing watches like this one as First World War pieces. They cannot be. Whatever West End’s earlier military history, the Secundus name itself does not begin until the 1930s. The brand’s heritage and this watch’s date are two different subjects, and collapsing them into one is how a false story starts. I had started one myself, in the subject line, before I knew better.

The rest of what they told me is context rather than provenance. It does not make my watch a soldier’s watch. It does something quieter and, to me, more interesting: it explains why a Swiss watch was circulating in this part of the world at all. West End did not sell to South Asia as an afterthought. South Asia was the business.

A Swiss factory in Bienne. Two addresses that mattered: Bombay and Calcutta.

Nine years of newsprint

The strongest evidence I have does not come from a dealer or a forum. It comes from The Indian Listener, the programme journal of All India Radio, where West End advertised for years, page after page, alongside cigarettes, radio valves, tyres and Benarasi sarees.

These are contemporary documents. They were printed while the watches were being sold, for people who might walk into a shop the next morning and buy one. Tap any of them to read the whole page.

What the advertisements actually prove

More than I expected, and less than I would like.

The August 1936 page settles the earliest question independently. Secundus was a named, advertised line by then, with four models, fifteen jewels and prices from Rs. 32 to Rs. 90. West End told me the 1930s; the 1936 page shows the 1930s, in dated print, without my having to take anyone’s word for it. A company remembering something and a page printed at the time are not the same kind of evidence.

But notice what is in those early pages: wrist watches. The 1936 page and the c. 1938 to 1939 page advertise Secundus for the wrist: tonneau cases, rectangular cases and Everbright steel backs. There is no pocket watch in either.

The pocket watch appears in February 1945. And when it appears, it is described with a precision that is almost unfair:

The Secundus Pocket

15 jewels · nickel silver · open face · with Roman or Arabic numerals

The Indian Listener, February 1945, page 19

Nickel. Open face. Arabic numerals offered as an option. That is this watch, item for item, in a wartime advertisement printed for readers in Bombay and Calcutta.

I want to be careful here, because this is exactly the point where a good story starts overtaking the evidence. A contemporary advertisement establishes that a configuration was being marketed at a given moment. It does not date an individual surviving example. Production runs span years. Components overlap. An illustration can stand for a family of watches rather than one reference.

So the defensible sentence is not “this watch was made in 1945.” It is this:

By 1945, West End was advertising a Secundus pocket watch whose specification matches this one exactly.

For an object with no papers, no owner and no date, that is a great deal.

The engineer and his watch

There is one page I keep going back to, and I should admit up front that my reasons for it are not evidential.

December 1944. The headline reads The Engineer. The illustration is a man at a machine in a workshop. The copy is about vibration, metallic dust in the air, hands and wrists constantly in motion and watches that have to survive all of it. The testimonial beside it is signed by a Captain of the Royal Engineers, describing a watch that had kept perfect time for years through heat, dust and sweat.

I am an engineer. I read that page and felt something I have no right to feel, because it proves nothing about this watch. It does not tell me who owned it. It does not put it in a workshop or a field camp or anyone’s waistcoat pocket.

What it does tell me is what kind of object this was meant to be. Not jewellery. An instrument, sold to people whose work depended on it, in a decade when there was no other way to know the time.

And there is something in the questions themselves. Why did it stop? Why did it run flat and fail upright? What is inside it? A mechanical movement is a small engineering system: energy stored, energy transmitted, energy released under control, oscillation regulated. Every part exists in relation to another, and when one fails the whole system tells you about it. The engineers reading that page in 1944 and the one holding this watch in Kathmandu in 2026 are not connected by provenance. We are connected by the same instinct to open the thing up and find out.

The numbers I cannot read

The outside of the caseback carries 876562. Inside, over a field of engine-turned guilloché, is V 6546, alongside a second set of scratched figures of the kind watch repairers have always left behind to record a service.

Every one of those looks like it should be an answer. None of them is, yet. A case number is not automatically a maker’s serial. An internal mark is not automatically a date. A number that resembles a sequence on some other surviving example may belong to a different system entirely. Without an authoritative numbering scheme or an archive to check them against, the honest thing is to record them exactly as they appear and leave them as evidence rather than decode them into a story.

One correction to my own account. When I wrote to Switzerland I said the movement carried no serial number. Looking at the photographs again, that is not quite right. There are two short lines of stamping on the plate beside the balance, too shallow and too worn to read at this angle. Whatever they say, they are the most promising thing left in the watch. They need raking light and a loupe.

Where the research stands

Established

  • A genuine West End Watch Co. Secundus mechanical pocket watch, Swiss made.
  • The Secundus line existed by August 1936, shown in dated print rather than only in company recollection.
  • West End built its commercial identity around Britain’s Indian market, trading from Bombay and Calcutta.
  • By February 1945 the company was advertising a Secundus pocket watch in nickel silver, open face, with an Arabic-numeral option.
  • Wartime advertising placed West End watches with soldiers as well as with engineers and mechanics.
  • The movement has been serviced and runs continuously again.

Reasonable

  • An individual date in the late 1930s or the 1940s.
  • That the February 1945 advertisement depicts this model or one extremely close to it.
  • That it reached this part of the world through the same Bombay and Calcutta trade that carried West End across the subcontinent.

What remains open is more gracefully said in a sentence than set out as a ledger. The year of manufacture is not established. No military issue is documented, and nothing ties the watch to a particular soldier or to a particular engineer. The case and internal markings have not been read against any authoritative scheme, of its life before mine, whose pocket and which city and how many decades, nothing at all is known. None of that is a deficiency in the object. It is the work that is left, and it is specific rather than vague: photograph the movement stamping under raking light, identify the calibre, find the case-maker’s mark, locate more period catalogues and approach the museum holding West End’s archive, which the company has confirmed exists and is not held at the factory. Until then the question mark stays. An honest question mark is worth more than an invented date.

Still ticking

I do not know who wound this watch first. I do not know whose pocket it lived in, or what it was used to be on time for, or how it travelled from a counter in Bombay or Calcutta to a table in Kathmandu.

I know it was made by a Swiss company that built its life around a market four thousand miles from its factory. I know its name was chosen for luck. I know that in the middle of a world war a version of it was advertised to people who needed a watch that simply worked.

And I know that at some point it stopped, and that nobody came for it, and that it sat somewhere for years being nothing to anyone, until it wasn’t.

There are watches that cost more than everything I own. None of them would have made me sit down and read a radio journal from 1936. This one is not rare and it is not valuable. It is the only object I have that outlived everybody who could explain it and still keeps time.
